# Which way would the line have to turn to face the person receiving the salute?

**Answer: to the right — toward the right-hand edge of the picture. That is roughly a
quarter turn (about 90°), clockwise if you imagine looking down on the parade ground
from above. And strictly speaking the line has already made that turn: the soldiers are
shown already facing the person they are saluting, who is standing just outside the
right-hand edge of the frame. The only thing pointing the "wrong" way is the camera,
which is off to the flank looking down the length of the line.**

## What the picture shows

A long line of soldiers — a couple of dozen or so men, in at least two ranks — in
olive-green fatigues and green berets (one man has a tan/khaki beret), drawn up at the
halt on a bare red-earth track, every one of them holding a salute with the hand at the
brow.

The line runs away from the camera. The nearest man stands at the left edge of the
frame and is the biggest figure in the shot; the men get steadily smaller and sit
progressively higher in the frame as the line recedes toward the upper right, and the
line ends about four-fifths of the way across the picture. Each man therefore hides most
of the man next to him, which is the classic look of a rank photographed from its flank
rather than from its front. Everything to the right of the end of the line is empty,
open red dirt, and the background is scrubby green bush and sky with no other people in
it.

## Which way the men are facing

Every soldier is in profile facing the **right** of the frame, and we are looking at
their right-hand sides, very slightly from the front:

- The heads are in right profile — forehead, nose and chin all point to the right, and
  the berets are pulled down over the right side with the crown draping forward to the
  right.
- The saluting arm is the right arm, and on every man it is on the near side of the
  body, raised and bent so that the hand sits against the right eyebrow, clearly
  overlapping the chest. If these men were facing left, we would be looking at their
  left sides and that arm and hand would be hidden behind the head instead of standing
  out in front of the body.
- The torsos read as narrow (a side-on view), with the shirt-front pockets and the
  buckled waist belts visible along the right-hand, leading edge of each silhouette —
  so we are seeing a sliver of the front of the uniform, not the back.
- The boots settle it. Each man is at attention with heels together and toes splayed,
  and every toe-cap in the line points out to the right of the frame (the nearer foot
  angled slightly toward the camera, the far foot slightly away).

## Where the person receiving the salute must be

A rank at the halt salutes to its front, so the recipient — the reviewing or inspecting
officer — is standing **off the right-hand edge of the photograph**, out on the swept,
empty red-earth ground that fills the right-hand side and right foreground of the
picture. That bare strip is precisely the open space kept clear in front of the troops.
He is at roughly "three o'clock" from the line, facing back toward it (that is, facing
to our left), at about the same sort of distance from the camera as the men themselves
— which is why he falls just outside the frame rather than appearing in the background.

## Stating the turn explicitly

- **Direction relative to the viewer: to the right.** Whichever way you frame the
  question, the recipient lies out beyond the right edge of the photo, so any turn is a
  turn to the right, not the left.
- **Size and sense of the turn:** about 90°, a quarter turn, clockwise as seen from
  overhead. The line currently stretches away from us toward the upper right; swinging
  it round so that it points at, or squares up to, the person off to the right means
  bringing the far end of the line round toward the camera and the near end round toward

- **But no turn is actually required.** The men are already halted facing their front,

  it only looks side-on because the photographer is standing on the flank, roughly 90°
  round from where the officer is. To look at the recipient yourself you would swing the
